title: Kimball Group, Dimensional Modeling Techniques (Overview)
text:
## Kimball Dimensional Modeling Techniques

The Kimball Group codified a set of official dimensional modeling techniques, drawn from The Data Warehouse Toolkit (Third Edition). These are the canonical vocabulary a top analyst uses when designing analytics-ready schemas.

## Fundamental Concepts

Business processes are the operational activities that the organization performs, and each generates measurable events. Dimensions provide the descriptive context (the who, what, where, when, why, how) surrounding a business process event. Facts are the measurements that result from a business process event, almost always numeric. The grain is the atomic level of detail: exactly what a single fact table row represents. Star schemas are the physical structure where a central fact table joins out to surrounding dimension tables; OLAP cubes are the analogous multidimensional structure.

## Basic Fact Table Techniques

Facts are classified by additivity. Additive facts can be summed across every dimension (for example, sales dollar amount). Semi-additive facts can be summed across some dimensions but not others, most commonly not across time (for example, account balances and inventory levels). Non-additive facts cannot be summed across any dimension (for example, ratios and unit prices); to aggregate them you sum the underlying additive components first, then compute the ratio.

There are three fundamental grains of fact table. Transaction fact tables record one row per measurement event at a point in space and time. Periodic snapshot fact tables capture the state of a process at regular, predictable intervals (daily, weekly, monthly). Accumulating snapshot fact tables track the progress of a process with a well-defined beginning and end through its milestones, with one row per instance and multiple date columns updated as the process advances. Factless fact tables record the occurrence of events or coverage conditions where no numeric measurement exists (for example, student attendance or promotion coverage). Conformed facts are facts that are defined identically across multiple fact tables so they can be compared and combined.

## Basic Dimension Table Techniques

Dimension surrogate keys are system-generated integer keys, meaningless in themselves, assigned to each dimension row; fact tables join to dimensions only via these surrogate keys. Natural keys are the operational business identifiers, durable keys are persistent identifiers that survive across source-system changes, and supernatural (durable) keys remain stable even as natural keys change. Degenerate dimensions are dimension attributes (like an order number or ticket number) that have no other attributes, so they are stored directly in the fact table without a separate dimension. Denormalized flattened dimensions store hierarchies as redundant columns in a single wide dimension table rather than normalizing (snowflaking) them out. Role-playing dimensions are a single physical dimension referenced multiple times in a fact table with different logical meanings (for example, order date, ship date, due date all referencing the date dimension). Junk dimensions consolidate a handful of low-cardinality flags and indicators into a single dimension rather than modeling each separately.

## Integration via Conformed Dimensions

Conformed dimensions are dimensions that mean the same thing, and share the same content and structure, across multiple fact tables and business processes; they are the foundation of enterprise integration and let analysts drill across processes. Shrunken rollup dimensions are conformed subsets of a base dimension at a higher level of aggregation (for example, a month dimension that conforms to the daily date dimension). The Enterprise Data Warehouse Bus Architecture is the framework of separately deliverable dimensional models tied together by shared conformed dimensions. The Enterprise Data Warehouse Bus Matrix is the primary planning tool: rows are business processes, columns are conformed dimensions, and cells mark which dimensions participate in which process, providing an incremental, integrated roadmap.

title: Kimball Group, Declaring the Grain
text:
## Declaring the Grain

Declaring the grain is the pivotal step in a dimensional design. The grain establishes exactly what a single fact table row represents. The grain declaration becomes a binding contract on the design: it must be determined before choosing dimensions or facts, because every candidate dimension or fact must be consistent with the declared grain.

## Why Grain Declaration Comes First

Declaring a consistent grain enforces a uniformity on all dimensional designs that is critical to BI application performance and ease of use. The most frequent design error by far is not declaring the grain of the fact table at the beginning of the design process. If the grain is not clearly defined, the whole design rests on quicksand: dimensions and facts get inconsistently mixed, and measurements can be inappropriately double counted.

## Atomic Grain

Atomic grain is the lowest level at which data is captured by a given business process. The grain is determined by the physical realities of the source of the data. Designs should start at the lowest, most atomic grain because atomic data withstands the assault of unpredictable, ad hoc user queries: it can be rolled up in every conceivable way. Higher summary grains are valuable for performance tuning but presume the business questions are already known, so they cannot answer new questions the way atomic data can. It is common to build fact tables at multiple grains (atomic plus one or more rollups) from the same source.

## Single Grain Discipline

Different grains must not be mixed in the same fact table. Each distinct grain belongs in its own physical fact table. Having the discipline to keep a single, uniform level of detail per fact table assures that measurements are not double counted when they are aggregated.

title: dbt Labs, Docs: Models
text:
## dbt Models

In dbt, a model is a single file that contains a final select statement, saved as a .sql (or .py) file. Models are the core of how dbt transforms data and are where analytics engineers spend most of their time. When you run dbt run, dbt takes the select statement in each model and wraps it in the boilerplate needed to build that result as a table or view in the data warehouse, without the data ever leaving the warehouse. Models perform the T (Transform) of the modern ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) workflow.

## SQL Models and ref

Most models are SQL select statements. The central mechanism that lets models build on each other is the ref function: instead of hard-coding a database schema and table name, one model selects from another with {{ ref('other_model') }}. This does two things: it tells dbt the dependency order in which to build models (constructing a directed acyclic graph, the DAG), and it inserts the correct, environment-specific relation name at compile time. Because dependencies are inferred from ref, dbt can build models in the right order and run independent branches in parallel. Python models (supported since dbt 1.3) are also allowed for transformations better expressed in Python, such as using specific packages, and they interoperate with SQL models via ref and dbt.ref inside the Python function.

## Materializations

Each model has a materialization that controls how dbt persists it in the warehouse. The main options are: view (the model is rebuilt as a view, cheap to build, computed at query time), table (the model is rebuilt as a table each run), incremental (dbt inserts or updates only new or changed rows since the last run, for large event-style tables), and ephemeral (the model is not built in the warehouse at all but inlined as a common table expression into downstream models). Materialization is set with a config block or in the project yml, and can be changed without rewriting the SQL.

## Project Structure and Modularity

Models live in a dbt project directory alongside a project yml. Because each model is one select and models reference each other through ref, complex pipelines are decomposed into small, single-purpose, modular transformations that are far easier to build, test, and reason about than a single monolithic query. A common layered convention is staging models (one per source table, light cleanup and renaming), intermediate models (business logic building blocks), and marts (the final fact and dimension tables the business consumes).

title: dbt Labs, Docs: Data Tests
text:
## dbt Data Tests

Data tests are assertions you make about your models and other resources in your dbt project (sources, seeds, snapshots). When you run dbt test, dbt tells you whether each test passes or fails. Under the hood a data test is a SQL select statement that seeks to grab failing records, the rows that disprove your assertion. If the test returns zero failing rows, it passes. This makes data quality checks a first-class, version-controlled, automatically-run part of the analytics codebase rather than an afterthought.

## Singular Data Tests

A singular data test is a one-off assertion written as a .sql file (typically in the tests/ directory), containing a single select statement that returns the offending rows. For example, a test that payments per order are never negative selects order_id and sum(amount) as total_amount from the payments fact, groups by order_id, and keeps only rows having total_amount < 0. Any rows returned are failures.

## Generic Data Tests

A generic data test is a parameterized, reusable test defined in a test block (similar to a macro) and then referenced by name in yml files on models, columns, sources, snapshots, and seeds. dbt ships with four built-in generic tests: unique (the column contains only unique values), not_null (the column contains no null values), accepted_values (every value is drawn from a specified list), and relationships (every value has a matching value in another model, enforcing referential integrity). Packages such as dbt_utils and dbt_expectations add many more.

## Defining Tests in YAML

Generic tests are attached to models and columns in the yml properties file under the data_tests key (the older key tests is still supported as an alias). For example, on an orders model: order_id has unique and not_null; status has accepted_values with values placed, shipped, completed, returned; customer_id has relationships to ref('customers') field id. In plain English these assert that order_id is unique and never null, status is always one of the four allowed values, and every customer_id in orders exists as an id in customers. Running these on every build catches broken assumptions (duplicated keys, orphaned foreign keys, unexpected category values) before they reach a dashboard.

title: dbt Labs, Docs: Sources
text:
## dbt Sources

Sources make it possible to name and describe the raw data that Extract and Load tools have loaded into your warehouse. By declaring tables as sources in dbt you can select from them in your models with the source() function (which defines lineage in the DAG), test assumptions about the source data, and calculate the freshness of the source data. Sources are the documented, tested entry point of the pipeline, so an analyst never selects from a raw table by a hard-coded name.

## Declaring Sources and the source() Function

Sources are declared in a yml file under a sources key: each source has a name, an optional database and schema, and a list of tables. In a model you reference a source table as {{ source('jaffle_shop', 'orders') }}, which dbt compiles to the fully-qualified relation such as raw.jaffle_shop.orders and records a dependency from the model to that source. If the physical table name differs from the logical name you set identifier on the table (for example identifier: api_orders).

## Testing and Documenting Sources

Because a source is a first-class resource, you attach descriptions and data tests to it in yml exactly as you would a model: a description on the source and each table, and column-level tests like unique and not_null on a primary key. This catches upstream data problems (duplicate keys, nulls) at the boundary before they propagate through the models.

## Source Freshness

dbt can monitor how stale the loaded data is. You set loaded_at_field to the timestamp column that records when each row landed, and a freshness config with warn_after and error_after thresholds expressed as a count and a period (for example warn_after 12 hours, error_after 24 hours). Running dbt source freshness issues a query taking max(loaded_at_field) versus the current timestamp; if the newest row is older than warn_after dbt warns, older than error_after it errors. Thresholds can be set per source and overridden per table, and freshness can be disabled on a table with freshness: null. You can then build only what is downstream of newly-refreshed sources with a selector like source_status:fresher+.

title: dbt Labs, Docs: About MetricFlow (Semantic Layer)
text:
## MetricFlow and the Semantic Layer

MetricFlow is a SQL query generation engine that powers the dbt Semantic Layer. It lets a team define the logic for the company's metrics once, in YAML, and then generate consistent SQL for those metrics across any slice of the data. The goal is a single source of truth for metric definitions: instead of every analyst re-deriving revenue or active users in each dashboard query (and quietly disagreeing), the definition lives in version-controlled code and every tool asks the Semantic Layer for the same answer.

## The Semantic Graph and Semantic Models

The semantic graph is the network of semantic models and their relationships, a subset of the dbt DAG where nodes are semantic models and edges are the join relationships between them. When MetricFlow builds a metric it uses this graph to find the correct join path between tables. A semantic model corresponds to a dbt model and contains three kinds of metadata: entities (the join keys, which are the traversal edges between semantic models), dimensions (the ways you group, slice, and filter metrics, such as date or customer type), and measures (the aggregatable quantities, defined as an aggregation like sum or count over a column).

## Metrics as a Single Source of Truth

Metrics are defined on top of measures and semantic models in YAML. Consider order_total: without a semantic layer, one analyst writes select date_trunc('day', ordered_at), sum(order_total) ... group by 1 and another writes a subtly different version, and the numbers drift. With MetricFlow the metric is defined once and reused across every query, dashboard, and downstream application, which gives consistency (everyone uses the same definition), maintainability (change it in one place and it propagates), and auditability (the logic is in git).

## Core Principles

MetricFlow follows a set of principles: flexibility with completeness (express metric logic as flexible abstractions over any data model), DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself, minimize redundant metric logic), simplicity with gradual complexity (start from familiar data-modeling concepts), and performance and efficiency. It is compatible with dbt 1.6 and higher and is open source under Apache 2.0. Normalized data is ideal but MetricFlow works with any dataset from raw to fully denormalized.

title: PostgreSQL Documentation, Tutorial: Window Functions
text:
## Window Functions

A window function performs a calculation across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. This is comparable to the type of calculation done with an aggregate function, but unlike ordinary aggregate functions a window function does not cause the rows to become grouped into a single output row: the rows retain their separate identities. Behind the scenes the window function is able to access more than just the current row of the query result. This is the tool that lets an analyst compute running totals, rankings, moving averages, and period-over-period comparisons without collapsing detail.

## The OVER Clause and PARTITION BY

A window function call always contains an OVER clause directly following the window function's name and arguments; this is what syntactically distinguishes it from a normal or aggregate function. The OVER clause determines how the query rows are split up for processing. The PARTITION BY list within OVER divides the rows into partitions (groups) that share the same values; the function is computed across the rows of the current row's partition. For example, avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY depname) compares each employee's salary to the average salary in their department while keeping one row per employee.

## ORDER BY Within the Window and Frames

ORDER BY inside OVER controls the order in which rows are processed within each partition; it need not match the query's output order. row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers rows 1, 2, 3 within each department from highest salary down. For each row there is a set of rows in its partition called the window frame. Some functions act only on the frame rather than the whole partition. By default, if ORDER BY is supplied, the frame runs from the start of the partition through the current row plus any following peers equal under the ORDER BY; if ORDER BY is omitted the frame is the whole partition. Thus sum(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary) produces a running total.

## Where Window Functions Are Allowed

Window functions are permitted only in the SELECT list and the ORDER BY clause of a query. They are forbidden in WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING, because they logically execute after those clauses have been processed. To filter on the result of a window function (for example, to keep only the top two salaries per department) you must wrap the window calculation in a subquery and filter in the outer query's WHERE. Named window definitions using a WINDOW clause let you reuse the same OVER specification across several functions.

title: dbt Labs, How We Style Our SQL
text:
## dbt SQL Style Guide

dbt Labs publishes an opinionated SQL style guide that top analytics engineers treat as a baseline for readable, reviewable, DRY SQL. Consistent style is not cosmetic: it makes SQL diffable in code review, easier to maintain, and less error-prone.

## Formatting Basics

Use a linter such as SQLFluff to enforce the rules automatically. Indent with four spaces and keep lines to about 80 characters. Write keywords, field names, and function names in lowercase. Use trailing commas, not leading commas. Always use the explicit as keyword when aliasing a field or table. Use Jinja comments {# #} for comments that should not appear in the compiled SQL.

## Fields, Aggregations, and Grouping

List plain fields before aggregates and window functions in the select. Aggregate as early as possible, on the smallest dataset, before joining. Group and order by column position numbers (group by 1, 2) rather than repeating column names. A key rule for analytics: do not use select *, name the columns you need, both to limit data scanned and to make the query's output explicit and stable.

## Joins

Prefer union all over union unless you specifically need to remove duplicates. When joining two or more tables, prefix every column with its full table name rather than a cryptic alias or initialism, so the reader knows where each column comes from. Write the explicit join type (inner join, not just join). Avoid right join; restructure it as a left join so the query reads left to right.

## CTEs (Common Table Expressions)

Structure models with CTEs. Put import CTEs at the top of the file, each pulling from a single {{ ref('...') }} or {{ source('...') }} and named after the table it references, selecting only the needed columns with any where filters applied early. Functional CTEs each do a single logical unit of work and get verbose, descriptive names (events_joined_to_users, not user_events). Refactor CTEs duplicated across models into their own intermediate model. End the model with a final CTE and a select from it, which makes the output easy to audit and swap during materialization testing.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Clutter-Free: One of the 3 Cs for Better Charts
text:
## Clutter-Free Charts and the Data-Ink Ratio

Nielsen Norman Group frames clutter as one of the three Cs of better charts. The organizing idea is Edward Tufte's data-ink ratio: the proportion of a visualization's ink that actually conveys information. Data ink is the core meaning, the marks that cannot be removed without changing the message; everything else is candidate for deletion. Tufte's rule, quoted here, is that data graphics should draw the viewer's attention to the sense and substance of the data, not to something else.

## Chartjunk as Noise

Chartjunk is any unnecessary visual element that distracts from meaning. Using a signal-to-noise framing, data ink is the signal and chartjunk is the noise; maximizing the data-ink ratio means suppressing the noise so the signal reads clearly. A high data-ink ratio is efficient communication with minimal redundancy.

## What to Remove

Avoid default spreadsheet styling such as funky colors, gradients, shadows, textures, and especially 3D effects, which obscure meaning and can create optical illusions that distort how magnitudes are perceived. Drop redundant axes and gridlines when the chart already shows exact data labels (but keep them when the reader needs to judge relative magnitude or read confidence intervals without precise numbers). Replace legends with direct labeling on the data series, which is both faster to read and friendlier to colorblind viewers because it removes the back-and-forth color matching. Omit axis titles when the chart title already makes the metric obvious.

## Guiding Principle

The philosophy is less is more: remove any visual element that does not serve the specific communication goal of the chart. Every stroke that is not doing work is competing with the strokes that are.

title: Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, Death to Pie Charts (storytelling with data)
text:
## Death to Pie Charts (Anti-Pattern)

Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, author of Storytelling with Data, argues bluntly against the pie chart. Her position: I hate pie charts, I mean really hate them, and the 3D exploding variant is the absolute worst. This is a widely cited statement of a classic visualization anti-pattern.

## The Perceptual Problem

The fundamental issue is that our eyes are not good at attributing quantitative value to two-dimensional spaces. A pie chart asks the reader to compare the areas and angles of wedges. When two slices are close in size it is nearly impossible to tell which is larger, and even when sizes differ clearly the reader can only judge that one is bigger, not by how much. Meaningless categorical colors make it worse: a darker slice can appear artificially larger, an optical illusion. And once you add data labels to compensate, the visual itself is no longer doing the communicating, so the chart is wasting space.

## The Recommended Alternative

Knaflic recommends replacing the pie with a horizontal bar chart sorted by value. Bars work because our eyes compare their end points against a common baseline, so it is easy to see both which category is largest and how much larger it is than the others. If you must keep a pie, at least make the slices a single color and highlight only the one or two you want the audience to focus on, rather than coloring every slice differently.

title: Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, My Guiding Principles (storytelling with data)
text:
## Guiding Principles for Communicating with Data

Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic distills data storytelling into a short set of guiding principles that top analysts internalize when they move from exploring data to explaining it.

## Be Clear on Your Intent

First decide whether you are visualizing for exploratory purposes (to understand the data yourself) or explanatory purposes (to make a specific point clear to someone else). Explanatory work demands a clear point of view: you are not dumping everything you found, you are making one thing land.

## The Right Graph Creates an Aha Moment

An effective visualization surfaces an insight that was not immediately obvious and makes the data's story feel intuitive rather than effortful to decode.

## Don't Overcomplicate, but Don't Oversimplify

The craft is taking intricate information and presenting it accessibly without dumbing it down. Avoid unnecessary complexity.

## Get Rid of the Non-Essential

Quoting Antoine de Saint-Exupery: you know you have achieved perfection not when you have nothing more to add, but when you have nothing to take away. Systematically remove clutter and distractions.

## Make It Clear Where to Look

Do not force the audience to process everything at once. Establish visual hierarchy: emphasize the critical elements and de-emphasize the rest so attention goes where you intend.

## Words Make a Graph Accessible

Text is not optional. Provide clear chart and axis titles, label the data source, note methodology, and spell out acronyms so the visual stands on its own.

## Audience Trumps All Else

Above every other consideration, meet the needs of your specific audience. The audience, not the analyst's preference, decides what good looks like.

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, What is EDA?
text:
## Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

The NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook defines Exploratory Data Analysis as an approach, or philosophy, for data analysis that employs a variety of techniques, mostly graphical, to maximize insight into a data set, uncover underlying structure, extract important variables, detect outliers and anomalies, test underlying assumptions, develop parsimonious models, and determine optimal factor settings. EDA is the disciplined habit of looking at data before modeling it, and it is a core competency for an analyst.

## EDA Is a Philosophy, Not Just Graphics

EDA is not identical to statistical graphics, although the two terms are used almost interchangeably. Statistical graphics is a collection of techniques (plots); EDA is a broader approach to how analysis proceeds. The distinguishing move of EDA is that it postpones the usual assumptions about what kind of model the data follow, and instead lets the data itself reveal its underlying structure and model. This contrasts with classical analysis, which imposes a model first and then estimates and tests it.

## Why Graphics

EDA relies heavily on graphical techniques because graphics give the analyst unparalleled power to explore data open-mindedly, and because they engage the analyst's natural pattern-recognition abilities to reveal unsuspected structure and insight. The staple EDA plots include the histogram, the probability plot, the lag plot, the box plot, and small multiples (positioning several plots together) to exploit the eye's ability to compare. In practice EDA is used to sanity-check data quality and distributions, spot outliers, and form hypotheses before any dashboard, metric, or model is built on top of the data.

title: Kimball Group, Slowly Changing Dimensions (Types 1, 2, 3)
text:
## Slowly Changing Dimensions

Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCDs) are the standard techniques for handling changes to dimension attribute values over time, for example an employee's home city changing or a product being recategorized. How you handle the change determines whether historical facts are reported against the old or the new attribute value, which is one of the most consequential modeling decisions an analyst makes.

## Type 1: Overwrite

With a Type 1 change, the old attribute value is simply overwritten with the new one; no history of the prior value is kept. Kimball's example: the Home City field for an employee changes from Santa Cruz to Boulder Creek, and the record is updated in place. Type 1 is appropriate for correcting errors and for situations where you consciously choose not to track history. The tradeoff is that Type 1 destroys the history of that field: any report that constrains or groups on Home City will change, because all past facts now roll up under the new value.

## Type 2: Add a Row

With a Type 2 change, you carefully keep track of the change by inserting a new dimension row with a new surrogate primary key to capture the changed state. Both the prior and new rows carry the natural key (or durable identifier), a most-recent-row flag, and row effective and expiration dates. Existing facts stay joined to the old surrogate key and new facts join to the new one, so history is preserved exactly: facts are reported against the attribute values that were in effect when they occurred. Type 2 is the workhorse for accurate change tracking.

## Type 3: Add a Column

With a Type 3 change, you add a new column to preserve the old attribute value while the main attribute is overwritten with the new value (as in Type 1). This creates an alternate reality that coexists with current truth: you can report by the current value or by the prior (for example current versus previous sales region), but it only remembers one prior state, not full history.

title: Kimball Group, Design Tip #152: SCD Types 0, 4, 5, 6, 7
text:
## Advanced Slowly Changing Dimension Types

Beyond the core Type 1, 2, and 3, Kimball catalogs additional SCD techniques for more demanding cases. Knowing all of them is a mark of dimensional-modeling depth.

## Type 0: Retain Original

The dimension attribute value never changes, so facts are always grouped by this original value. Type 0 is used for attributes explicitly labeled original (such as original credit score), for durable identifiers, and for most date-dimension attributes, which are fixed by definition.

## Type 4: Add Mini-Dimension

A group of rapidly changing or frequently analyzed dimension attributes is split off into a separate mini-dimension. This is used when attribute values are volatile or when heavily used attributes live in a very large dimension. Each unique combination of the mini-dimension attributes gets its own surrogate key, and both the base dimension key and the mini-dimension key are captured in the fact table.

## Type 5: Add Mini-Dimension and Type 1 Outrigger

Type 5 builds on Type 4 by embedding a current profile mini-dimension key in the base dimension, maintained as a Type 1 attribute (overwritten). This lets you get the current attribute values directly from the base dimension without going through the fact table. The outrigger attributes are given distinct names (such as Current Income Level) to separate them from the historical mini-dimension attributes.

## Type 6: Add Type 1 Attributes to a Type 2 Dimension

Type 6 combines Type 2 historical tracking with embedded current attributes in the same dimension, so facts can be filtered or grouped by either the historical value or the current value. When the attribute changes, the current-value columns are updated across all prior Type 2 rows for that entity.

## Type 7: Dual Type 1 and Type 2 Dimensions

The fact table carries dual foreign keys: one surrogate key to the Type 2 dimension row (historical view) and one durable key resolving to the current row (current view). This delivers Type 6 style dual perspective through separate keys rather than by physically overwriting current-value columns.

title: Stephen Few, Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design (Perceptual Edge)
text:
## Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design (Anti-Patterns)

Stephen Few, in his Perceptual Edge white paper and in Information Dashboard Design, catalogs the thirteen most common mistakes in dashboard design. A dashboard, in Few's definition, is a visual display of the most important information needed to achieve one or more objectives, consolidated on a single screen so it can be monitored at a glance. Most of these pitfalls are anti-patterns a top analyst actively avoids.

## The Thirteen Pitfalls

Exceeding the boundaries of a single screen: forcing the viewer to scroll or navigate to other screens fragments the picture and hides connections that should be seen together at a glance. Supplying inadequate context for the data: a number like 8.3 million means little without a comparison, a target, or a trend to judge it against. Displaying excessive detail or precision: too many decimal places or overly granular figures slow the reader without adding meaning. Choosing a deficient measure: showing a metric that does not actually reflect what matters. Choosing inappropriate display media: for example using a pie chart or a gauge where a bar or line would communicate better. Introducing meaningless variety: using many different chart types just for visual variety rather than for fit to the data. Using display media ineffectively: even the right chart type poorly configured fails. Encoding quantitative data inaccurately: such as truncating a bar chart's value axis so it does not start at zero, distorting the comparison. Arranging the data poorly: ignoring importance and relationships in the layout. Highlighting important data ineffectively or not at all: everything equally weighted means nothing stands out. Cluttering the display with useless decoration (chartjunk). Misusing or overusing color: color with no meaning, or too many colors, adds noise. Designing an unattractive visual display: aesthetics affect trust and usability. The unifying lesson is that a dashboard must communicate the right information clearly and immediately, so every element must earn its place.

title: Wikipedia, Cohort Analysis
text:
## Cohort Analysis

Cohort analysis is a kind of behavioral analytics that breaks the data in a data set into related groups before analysis. These groups, or cohorts, usually share common characteristics or experiences within a defined time span. Typical cohorts are users who signed up in the same week or month, or customers acquired through the same channel or after a particular product upgrade. Instead of collapsing everyone into one average, the analyst tracks each cohort separately over its lifecycle.

## Why Cohorts Beat Blended Averages

The technique lets a company see patterns clearly across the lifecycle of a customer or user, rather than slicing across all customers blindly. A single blended metric (for example overall active users) can look flat or healthy while newer cohorts are actually retaining far worse than older ones; the aggregate hides the decline because large, older, well-retained cohorts mask it. Splitting by cohort exposes whether a product change helped or hurt the users who experienced it.

## Actionable vs Vanity Metrics

Cohort analysis is contrasted with vanity metrics such as total cumulative website hits or total registered users, which only ever go up and document the current state without revealing cause. An actionable metric ties specific and repeatable actions to observed results, so you can tell what to change. Cohort retention curves (what fraction of each signup cohort is still active in week 1, 2, 4, 8) are the classic actionable view, revealing whether the product is getting stickier over time and where in the lifecycle users are lost.

title: Mixpanel, Introduction to Funnel Analysis
text:
## Funnel Analysis

A funnel is a sequential series of steps that visualize a user flow to conversion. The steps can happen inside or outside the product and end in a conversion outcome such as a signup, a purchase, or completing a game level. Funnel analysis is the process of understanding who converts across each step of your funnel, and why, so you can discover the key drivers of conversion and optimize funnel performance. It is the standard analyst tool for diagnosing where a multi-step flow leaks users.

## Conversion, Windows, and Drop-off

Each step is a measurable event. The funnel reports the conversion rate from one step to the next: if only 50 percent of users who reached a step advance to the following step, half dropped off there. A conversion window sets how much time a user has after entering the funnel to still be counted as converting; the same sequence can look very different under a one-hour versus a seven-day window. Funnel analysis helps you figure out which users are more likely to convert, what causes drop-off, and what dropped-off users do instead.

## Segmenting to Find the Real Problem

The most valuable move is to break the funnel down by user characteristics or behaviors, so you can see which segments convert best and worst. Mixpanel's example filters a funnel by platform and finds that web users abandon short-form content more than mobile users, pinpointing a specific, fixable friction rather than a vague overall drop. The order of steps and the definition of the entry event matter: sloppy event definitions produce misleading funnels.

title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, Measures of Location
text:
## Measures of Location (Central Tendency)

The NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook defines the core measures of location an analyst uses to summarize where a distribution is centered. Choosing the right one, and knowing how each behaves with messy data, is basic analytical literacy.

## Mean

The mean is the sum of the data points divided by the number of data points: Ybar = (sum of Yi from i = 1 to N) / N. It is the most familiar average, but it lacks robustness of validity for non-normal distributions and is adversely affected by extreme values in the tails. A few very large or very small values pull the mean toward them, which is why a mean income or mean session length can be badly misleading on a skewed distribution.

## Median

The median is the value of the point which has half the data smaller than it and half larger. For an odd count N it is the middle ordered value Y at position (N+1)/2; for an even N it is the average of the two middle values. Because it is based on rank order rather than the actual magnitudes, the median has robustness of validity: extreme values do not distort it. For skewed real-world data (revenue, latency, order value) the median is usually the more honest summary.

## Mid-range

The mid-range is (smallest + largest) / 2. It is not robust, since it depends entirely on the two most extreme points, and is only appropriate when those extremes are themselves the analytically relevant quantities. The broader lesson for an analyst: always know whether a reported average is a mean or a median, and prefer the median when the distribution is skewed or contains outliers.

title: Wikipedia, Correlation Does Not Imply Causation
text:
## Correlation Does Not Imply Causation (Anti-Pattern)

Correlation does not imply causation refers to the inability to legitimately deduce a cause-and-effect relationship between two variables solely on the basis of an observed association between them. It is a questionable-cause logical fallacy, known in Latin as cum hoc ergo propter hoc (with this, therefore because of this). Presenting a correlation to stakeholders as if it proved causation is one of the most damaging mistakes an analyst can make, because it drives wrong decisions.

## Correlation Versus Causation

Correlation describes two variables moving together; causation means one variable directly produces a change in the other. Two variables changing together does not prove one causes the other. Correlation is still valuable as evidence for prediction, but establishing causation requires more: a temporal sequence (cause before effect), a plausible mechanism, and the elimination of alternative explanations.

## The Three Alternative Explanations

Reverse causation: the causal arrow runs the other way. For example, low cholesterol correlates with higher mortality, but underlying diseases that lower cholesterol are what drive the deaths, not the low cholesterol itself. Confounding (a hidden third variable) causes both observed phenomena: ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer because heat drives both, ice cream does not cause drowning. Coincidence: two unrelated variables line up by chance, and the more variable pairs you examine, the more spurious correlations you will find purely at random. The analyst's discipline is to look for confounders, consider reverse causation, and label observational findings as associations, not causes.

title: dbt Labs, How We Structure Our dbt Projects
text:
## Structuring an Analytics Project (Staging, Intermediate, Marts)

dbt Labs' canonical project structure describes a cohesive arc that moves data from source-conformed (shaped by external systems outside your control) to business-conformed (shaped by the concepts and definitions your organization creates). Transformations are organized into three layers in the models directory, each building on the last.

## Staging: Atomic Building Blocks

Staging models create the initial modular building blocks from raw source data: one staging model per source table, named stg_[source]_[entity], doing only light standardization (renaming columns, casting types, basic cleaning). They are the clean atoms all downstream work builds on. Nothing joins raw source tables directly; everything selects from staging.

## Intermediate: Purpose-Built Steps

Intermediate models stack layers of logic with clear, specific purposes, preparing staging models to be joined into business entities. The key discipline is DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): each transformation is applied in only one place, then reused, rather than being copy-pasted into many final queries.

## Marts: Business-Defined Entities

Marts bring the modular pieces together into wide, rich representations of the entities the business cares about (customers, orders), ready for analytics and reporting. These are the fact and dimension tables analysts and BI tools consume.

## Core Principles

Four principles govern the structure: modularity (stack transformations so logic is written once and reused), single source of truth (a disciplined layout ensures each piece of business logic lives in exactly one place, so a metric is defined once, not re-derived in every dashboard), consistency (explicit documented naming conventions so the team spends its decision bandwidth on real problems, not folder layout), and comprehensibility (the codebase and the data both tell a clear story and stay approachable at scale).

title: Financial Times, Visual Vocabulary (chart selection)
text:
## The Visual Vocabulary: Choosing the Right Chart

The Financial Times graphics team's Visual Vocabulary organizes chart types by the relationship the analyst needs to communicate, not by what looks nice. It defines nine categories, each answering a different question, and lists the appropriate chart forms for each. Picking the chart from the message (rather than reaching by default for a bar or pie) is a hallmark of skilled data communication.

## The Nine Categories

Deviation: emphasise variations, plus or minus, from a fixed reference point (diverging bar, diverging stacked bar, spine chart, surplus/deficit line). Correlation: show the relationship between two or more variables, while noting readers may wrongly assume causality (scatterplot, line plus column, connected scatterplot, bubble, XY heatmap). Ranking: highlight an item's position in an ordered list when the position matters more than the absolute value (ordered bar, ordered column, dot strip plot, slope, lollipop). Distribution: show values and how often they occur, letting the shape or skew reveal inequality or lack of uniformity (histogram, boxplot, violin, population pyramid, dot plot, cumulative curve). Change over time: emphasise changing trends across time (line, column, area, stock price, slope, fan chart, calendar heatmap). Magnitude: show size comparisons of counted numbers, not calculated rates (column, bar, paired column, proportional symbol, isotype, radar). Part-to-whole: show how a single entity breaks into its components (stacked column, proportional stacked bar, pie, donut, treemap, waterfall). Spatial: emphasise precise location or geographic patterns when place matters most (choropleth, proportional symbol map, flow map, cartogram, dot density). Flow: show volumes or intensity of movement between states or conditions (Sankey, chord, network, waterfall).

## Why It Matters

Start from the story: is it a deviation, a ranking, a distribution, a part-to-whole? The category selects a small set of appropriate charts, which prevents the two classic errors of using a part-to-whole pie when you actually want a ranking, or a correlation scatter implying a cause you have not established.

title: Amplitude, User Retention (definition and measurement)
text:
## User Retention

User retention is how many active users continue to log in or use your product over a specified period, typically measured monthly, quarterly, and yearly for subscription products. Retention is the metric that matters most for durable growth: acquiring users is wasted if they do not come back.

## Retention Rate and Churn

A common retention rate formula is (users at end of period minus new users acquired during the period) divided by total users at the start of the period, expressed as a percentage. Churn rate is the inverse: retention plus churn equals 100 percent for a given cohort and period. The subtraction of new users is important, without it, new acquisition can mask the loss of existing users.

## Three Ways to Measure Retention

N-day retention (return on day N) measures whether a user is active on a specific day after day 0, for example day 1, day 7, day 30; it suits products with an expected daily or regular cadence. Unbounded retention (return on or after) counts a user as retained if they come back on a given day or any day after it, which suits products used irregularly such as grocery delivery, where N-day would understate real retention. Bracketed retention (return during custom ranges) groups days into custom buckets (for example days 1 to 3, 4 to 7, 8 to 14) to see where in the lifecycle users lose interest. Choosing the wrong definition for the product's natural usage frequency is a classic analytics mistake that makes a healthy product look like it is churning.

title: Kimball Group, The Three Fact Table Types
text:
## The Three Types of Fact Table

Kimball identifies three fundamental types of fact table. Almost every measurement in an analytics warehouse fits one of them, and choosing the right type is a core modeling decision.

## Transaction Fact Table

A row in a transaction fact table corresponds to a measurement event at a point in space and time, at the atomic transaction grain. These are the most dimensional and expressive fact tables, with robust dimensionality. They always include foreign keys for the associated dimensions and may optionally contain precise timestamps and degenerate dimension keys. Transaction fact tables may be dense or sparse, because a row exists only if a measurement actually took place. The measured numeric facts must be consistent with the transaction grain. This is the workhorse for detailed, drill-anywhere analysis.

## Periodic Snapshot Fact Table

A row in a periodic snapshot fact table summarizes many measurement events occurring over a standard period, such as a day, a week, or a month. The grain is the period, not the individual transaction. These tables tend to have many facts, since any measurement consistent with the grain is allowed, and dense foreign keys, because a row is inserted for every period even when nothing happened (with zero or null values). Periodic snapshots suit measures like balances and levels that are naturally sampled at regular intervals; such measures are typically semi-additive (summable across most dimensions but not across time).

## Accumulating Snapshot Fact Table

A row in an accumulating snapshot fact table summarizes the measurement events occurring at predictable steps between the beginning and the end of a process. There is a date foreign key in the fact table for each critical milestone in the process. Uniquely among the three types, the row is revisited and updated as the process advances: it is inserted when the process starts (for example when an order line is created) and updated as pipeline progress occurs. These tables model pipeline or workflow processes with a defined start, standard intermediate steps, and a defined end (order fulfillment, claim processing), and often include numeric lag measurements between milestones and milestone completion counters.

title: CloverDX, The Dimensions of Data Quality
text:
## Dimensions of Data Quality

Data quality is assessed along a set of named dimensions, aligned with the DAMA framework, that give an analyst a vocabulary for exactly how data can be wrong. Every dashboard rests on these: a metric is only as trustworthy as the data feeding it.

## The Core Dimensions

Accuracy: accurate data reflects the real world, is factual and up to date, and serves as reliable information you can trust. Completeness: data is complete when all the necessary data is available and critical fields are populated (though not every field must be filled). Consistency: consistent data means all instances agree across multiple data sets, with values taken from different sources not conflicting with one another. Timeliness: minimizing latency so the data is with the right people at the right time, and its actual arrival matches the expected arrival. Validity: how well data conforms to business rules such as the required format, type, and range (for example a date that is a valid calendar date). Uniqueness: each real-world record occurs only once, avoiding the duplication that creates conflicting versions of the truth.

## Additional Dimensions

Relevancy: whether the data actually matters for the use case, so effort is not spent processing information no one needs. Auditability: being able to track how data is used and what changes were made, so important information is not silently overwritten. In practice these dimensions map directly onto tests an analyst automates: not_null and completeness ratios (completeness), unique and primary-key tests (uniqueness), accepted_values and range checks (validity), reconciliation across sources (consistency), and freshness checks (timeliness).
